header.tag_why: The rep had the deal at 20 percent until Wen rebuilt the cost of manual matching from the customer's own statements and the CFO called it "my number, not yours"; the reconciliation capability opened the door, but the business case built from her own data closed it.

messaging_changes.current_line: Every payout reconciles automatically to its transactions and your ERP.
messaging_changes.change: For finance buyers (CFO, controller) at regional B2B and distribution companies, open the first call with this line instead of M1: "Know where every deposit came from: each one matched to its transactions and to the invoice in your ERP, without the month-end archaeology." Use "deposits" rather than "payouts" with finance audiences. Do not claim it fixes the whole close.
messaging_changes.why: Reconciliation was the only part of the demo that got a reaction, and the CFO stopped the demo to go back to it (E25, E26). She talked about "the deposits" and wanting to know "where my money is," not about payouts (E42, E43, E7), and manual matching was only part of a nine-day close (E6).

messaging_changes.current_line: Proven ROI, backed by an independent economic impact study.
messaging_changes.change: For finance buyers: "Send us one month of your statements and we'll show you your own cost of manual matching: your number, not ours." Offer the one-month statement teardown as a standard step early in the sale, not as a late rescue.
messaging_changes.why: The deal went from "dead" at 20 percent to paperwork after a single working session on one month of the customer's own statements (E35, E28, E34). The CFO valued that it was "my number, not yours" (E32), which works against leading with an independent study.

messaging_changes.current_line: Financial infrastructure to grow globally, in every currency.
messaging_changes.change: Stop opening first calls with M1 for regional, single-country B2B and distribution buyers. Move it and the M2 developer story to an appendix or a later IT conversation, and lead with the reconciliation line (M9) instead.
messaging_changes.why: The standard "financial infrastructure, global growth, all the currencies" opener got silence (E21). This buyer's four-person IT team "aren't building anything" (E24), and "nobody said 'infrastructure'" during the deal (E43).

messaging_changes.current_line: Support plans with tiered response times, up to 24/7 coverage.
messaging_changes.change: Against bank-bundled incumbents, lead support messaging with "A named contact who knows your account, not a bank rep who changes without telling you," with tiered response times as the supporting detail. Use this only where the plan actually includes a named contact. When the incumbent offers "we can look at your rates," answer with visibility ("we show you where your money is") plus the named contact, not a discount.
messaging_changes.why: After talking to her bank, the CFO's one new question was whether she would get a named contact (E19), because her bank rep had changed and she didn't know the new one (E20). The incumbent's rate-review offer missed her actual concern (E16, E17).

trigger.insight: The inbound said portal, but the real trigger was a new CFO's painful first close; the portal was a low-stakes, off-the-shelf project (the rep's own "they were building a portal" collapses into "they aren't building anything"). Reconciliation was only "a chunk" of the nine-day close, so we should not claim we fix the whole close. Inbound form text told us the channel, not the pain, and we took it at face value for three calls.
trigger.messaging: For mid-market B2B inbound, add a discovery hook aimed at finance ("How long did your last month-end close take, and who matches deposits?") before any checkout pitch, and frame M9 around the close rather than around payments.

decider.insight: The economic buyer was the CFO, not IT, and our default motion (dev story, checkout proposal to the IT director) cost three dead weeks. She judged the proposal on its first page, so the first page decides whether a finance buyer engages. The rep's "thank god" admits that our standard opener would have hurt us in front of the actual decider.
decider.messaging: Create a finance-buyer proposal template whose first page states the reconciliation and close-time problem in the CFO's own numbers, and keep APIs/checkout in an appendix.

competitor.insight: The incumbent's only recorded move was to offer a rate review when the problem was visibility, so price was never the battleground and discounting would have answered the wrong question. The rep says the questions changed "not much," yet the bank contact led directly to a new question about a named contact. The incumbent's weakness was relationship turnover, not product. We know nothing about what Fiserv actually showed.
competitor.messaging: Against bank-bundled incumbents, answer "we can look at your rates" with "we show you where your money is" plus a named contact, and turn M5's generic tiered response times into a named-owner commitment.

message.insight: M1 (global, every currency) and M2 (developers) both landed as silence with a three-state distributor that has a four-person IT team. The only line that got a reaction was M9, ninth in our list, and the CFO physically stopped the demo for it. Our deck order is upside down for this segment.
message.messaging: For regional B2B and distribution, open with M9 reconciliation (deposit to transaction to ERP invoice) and drop M1 and M2 from the first call.

decided.insight: The swing from "dead" to paperwork came from one working session on one month of her own statements, not from the demo. She explicitly valued that the number was hers, which directly undercuts M6's "independent economic impact study." The figure that won the deal is not on record: the rep remembers only "something like 60 hours" and "low six figures."
decided.messaging: Replace M6's study-backed ROI claim with an offer: "Send us one month of statements and we'll show you your own cost of manual matching," and make the one-month data teardown a standard sales step.

gaps.insight: M8's proof library has no wholesale or invoice-driven customer, and a retail case study actively signalled that we didn't understand her business. She signed anyway, but raising it twice means it was a real objection, and we got past it only because of her own data. The 14 branch counters got a claim on a slide, not a demo, so M3 is unproven for this account and may become a post-sale risk.
gaps.messaging: Build a distributor/wholesale reference and case story centred on invoice reconciliation, and back M3 for B2B counter sales with a demo showing card-present payments landing in the same reconciliation report.

language.insight: The buyer's frame was visibility and cash location ("where my money is," "the deposits"), not payments, infrastructure or rates. Even M9's "payout" is our word: she talks about deposits arriving from the bank. Every top-line word in our messaging was absent from her vocabulary.
language.messaging: Rewrite M9 in buyer language, e.g. "Know where every deposit came from: matched to the transaction and the invoice, without the month-end archaeology," and test "deposits" over "payouts" with finance audiences.

gaps.question: What exactly was the hours and dollar figure Wen built, and how was it calculated?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Wen for the model and the final number (hours, loaded cost, unmatched-deposit write-offs) so we can turn it into a reusable template and a proof point.

gaps.question: What did Fiserv or the bank actually propose beyond a rate review?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Ines (or Paul) in a post-sale check-in whether the bank came back with anything else and what nearly kept them with the incumbent.

gaps.question: What changed in the customer's questions after she talked to the bank?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Dana whether anything beyond the named-contact question came up (contract terms, bank relationship, switching risk) and how much weight Ines gave the named contact.

gaps.question: Are the 14 branch counters (card-present) in scope of the signed deal, or still on the incumbent?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Dana to confirm from the contract and rollout plan, and ask Wen what was actually committed beyond the slide.

gaps.question: Why did she sign without the distributor reference, and what would the reference have needed to show?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Ines in a win interview what she wanted to hear from another distributor, so we know what the case study should prove.

gaps.question: How did Dana reach the CFO on the third call: who brought her in and what prompted it?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Dana what changed on call three, so the path to the finance buyer becomes repeatable in discovery.

close.rep_takeaway: The deal turned the moment you stopped pitching what the inbound asked for and started measuring what the CFO felt: one month of her statements beat the whole standard deck. In discovery, ask who owns the cost of the problem and how long their last close took. Bring the data teardown forward instead of saving it for a rescue. And write down the number that wins the deal, because the next rep needs it.
